sheet.line: Sweet Potato Pot de Crème: Miso, Cinnamon, Marshmallow Fluff

facts.text: Pot de creme is French for pot of cream, the cream meaning custard: a loose French dessert custard dating to the 17th century (one source), baked until just set, usually in a water bath, and served in the small pot or ramekin it was baked in. The English word is first recorded in 1941.

Miso in desserts brings salt and savoury depth; white (shiro) miso is the mildest and sweetest kind and the usual choice, most often in a miso caramel; pastry cooks warn that too much overwhelms a sweet dish. Miso is a Japanese paste of soybeans fermented with salt and koji.

Marshmallow Fluff is a marshmallow creme made in Lynn, Massachusetts. The recipe was first sold door to door in Somerville around 1917 and bought by two candy makers of Lynn, H. Allen Durkee and Fred Mower, whose partnership dates to 1920; Durkee-Mower still makes it in Lynn. A New Jersey company also claims the name from 1910.

The first documented recipe for mashed sweet potatoes baked under a marshmallow topping appeared in 1917, in a recipe booklet the Angelus Marshmallow company commissioned from Janet McKenzie Hill of the Boston Cooking School Magazine to sell more marshmallows; Angelus, later Campfire, printed sweet potato and marshmallow casseroles again in 1930 and 1950, and the dish became a Thanksgiving habit.
